analysis.one_liner: Lets victims of fake AI-generated sexual images sue for damages and court orders to remove them.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had bipartisan support from 14 cosponsors, never left the House Judiciary Committee and died when the Congress ended without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The DEFIANCE Act would let anyone whose likeness is used in a fake, sexually explicit image or video — often made with AI tools — sue the people who knowingly made, shared, or solicited it. Victims could collect up to $150,000 in damages plus attorney fees, sue under a pseudonym to protect their privacy, and get court orders forcing the fake images taken down. The bill amends an existing 2022 law covering non-consensual intimate images to cover AI-generated forgeries.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of non-consensual intimate images and 'deepfake' pornography — overwhelmingly women and girls, including people targeted by ex-partners, online harassers, or strangers using AI image tools. Today many have no practical legal remedy against anonymous posters; this would give them a federal lawsuit with real money damages, fee-shifting so lawyers can take cases, and ten years to file. Anyone who has been made the subject of an AI-generated sexual image without their consent would gain a cause of action, including people whose images were altered rather than fully fabricated.

how_it_helps.text: Defines a 'digital forgery' as any AI-created or manipulated intimate depiction of an identifiable person that looks authentic, whether or not it is labeled fake, and lets that person sue.
Victims can recover actual damages or $150,000 in liquidated damages, plus attorney fees and litigation costs, and can seek court orders to stop display or disclosure of the image.
Courts can protect plaintiffs' privacy by allowing pseudonyms, sealing personal information, and keeping control of the images themselves with the court.
Victims have up to ten years from discovery of the violation — or from turning 18 — to file, and the bill explicitly leaves stronger state and tribal laws in place rather than overriding them.
Liability reaches not just those who disclose the images but those who knowingly produce or possess them with intent to disclose, and those who solicit them.

analysis.who_pays: People who create, share, or solicit non-consensual AI-generated sexual images would face federal lawsuits with heavy damages. Some cost also falls on tech and AI companies whose tools or websites are used to make and spread such content, since liability follows the conduct, and on anyone contesting such suits. Court system resources absorb the litigation.

drawbacks.text: Critics raised First Amendment concerns that a ban covering any AI-manipulated intimate image 'indistinguishable' from an authentic one could sweep in protected speech such as satire or art, inviting constitutional challenges.
The $150,000 statutory penalty applies per violation regardless of the defendant's intent to profit, which a good-faith critic could call disproportionate for minor or accidental infringements.
Enforcement is practically hard: most offenders are anonymous or overseas, so even a strong law may not reach many of the people who actually produce these images.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: it gives victims of a fast-growing, genuinely harmful practice a legal tool they largely lack today, with privacy protections built in for the victims themselves. The main risks are overbreadth challenges and the difficulty of collecting judgments from anonymous actors, but the bill includes a knowledge requirement, a ten-year window, and savings clauses for state law that address the most common objections. On balance, a reasonably designed remedy rather than a badly designed one.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced the bill on March 6, 2024, joined by original cosponsors from both parties, including Republicans Mike Garcia, Nancy Mace, Lori Chavez-DeRemer, and Max Miller.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on the day of introduction.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and it never received consideration on the House floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The cosponsor list grew to 14, split evenly between 7 Republicans and 7 Democrats, yet the bipartisan support was never translated into committee or floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The people who make and spread non-consensual AI sexual images are better off, since no federal civil remedy now exists; so are the online platforms that profit from traffic to such content.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no roll-call record exists; sponsorship was bipartisan, with 7 Republicans and 7 Democrats among the 14 cosponsors.

industries.industry: AI image-generation and synthetic media tools
industries.note: The bill creates lawsuits against anyone who knowingly uses such tools to produce sexual images of identifiable people without consent, a market segment that thrives on traffic from exactly that use. Its interest in avoiding liability runs against the victims the bill protects.

industries.industry: Online platforms and websites hosting user content
industries.note: The bill targets the people who make, share, and solicit the images rather than the platforms that host them, so direct liability is limited. Platforms would still face takedown pressure through court injunctions and lose a revenue stream from this content.
